newsitem.title: UK: British politics plays second fiddle to May Day.
newsitem.headline: British politics plays second fiddle to May Day.

text.p: Villagers across Britain were celebrating with parties on Thursday, but it had nothing to do with the ruling Conservatives, opposition Labour or minority Liberal Democrats.
It was election day throughout the country, but in Rochester, Padstow and other towns politics played second fiddle to the traditional May Day festivities.
Long before people cast votes to choose the country's leader, they celebrated nature and welcomed the coming of spring with traditional songs and dances around a Maypole.
"It may be election day but it won't make any difference to our May Day celebrations," said a spokeswoman for the tourist board in the picturesque fishing village of Padstow.

May Day is so important in Padstow, on the western tip of Britain, that the local council changed the polling stations so the voting would not interfere with the dances of the giant blue and red hobby horses, a unique feature of local celebrations.
In line with tradition, strong men took turns manning the horses and most of the villagers had the day off to celebrate what it considers the most important day of the year.

"As far as I know it's never happened before. It's the first time there has been an election on May Day," she added. "People will be dancing around the town all day and will cast their vote as they get nearer to the polling stations."

May Day celebrations date back to the 14th century. The ancient custom of dancing round the Maypole is the centrepiece of most festivities along with Morris dancing -- English folk dances performed by people in fancy costumes.
Rochester, in southeastern England, welcomed May Day and the start of its five-day festival with a dawn awakening ceremony with the Jack-in-the-Green, a classic Victorian May Day figure.
"It dates back to pre-history," explained stone mason Terry Pearson. "It's a sign of spring, fertility and growth."

As the sun came up over Bluebell Hill, about 400 people watched the Green Man pop out of a seven-foot (two metre) high bush as teams of Morris dancers with bells jangling from their ankles pranced around it.

"The Green Man features in history going back to the Egyptians or whatever," said Chris Brisley, a regular at the early morning bash. "There has apparently been spring awakening ceremonies for centuries. It's traditional." Some 127 teams of Morris dancers took part in the festival, dressed as chimney sweeps, spring maidens and court jesters.
Dancer Susan Kensley said she had never voted.
"I don't really care about the election, to tell the truth. I'd rather come out dancing than vote," said the 27-year-old.
An official at the local polling station opposite the mediaeval castle described voter turnout by midday as moderate.

Indeed, thoughts of candidates and constituencies were far from their minds as the dawn crowd headed towards the ancient High Street -- festooned with banners and flowers -- in a rowdy parade to make sure the rest of Rochester knew it was May Day.

"It (voting) is a bit of a stupid way to spend such a nice day. It's not a serious day. It's a day for enjoying life, being comfy, well-fed and randy," said Ronald Hutton, a professor of history and an expert on mediaeval festivals.

The Puritans tried to ban Maypole dancing because of its supposed sexual connotations but Hutton argued that May Day ceremonies had nothing to do with fertility. "What people are celebrating is not so much trying to make the land fertile as being happy about the fact that winter is over completely, good times are coming back."
